A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Rodimus/Rodimus+ research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training, downstream evaluations, MQAR and NeedleBench results, architectural ablations, and practical math/code evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds controlled larger-model comparisons, additional recall benchmarks, efficiency measurements, and Rodimus+-Coder evaluations.

M1.justification: The core DDTS mechanism, SW-SKA, recurrent updates, and Rodimus+ architecture remain unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization for Rodimus+-Coder Chat variants, a limited extension of the practical-model training procedure described in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds FDA, SWDE, SQuADv2, NQ, TriviaQA, and DROP evaluations, extending recall coverage to medical reports, HTML extraction, and question answering. Its Coder evaluations also expand beyond v1's HumanEval/MBPP coverage to multilingual coding, code reasoning and repair, and text-to-SQL tasks, including MultiPL-E, CRUXEval, HumanEvalFix, and Spider.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds RecurrentGemma-2B. The practical-model comparison replaces v1's Qwen2, RWKV6, and Llama3.2 comparators with Qwen2.5-Coder variants, Gemma3, and Phi-4-Mini, while retaining Gemma2 in the expanded base/chat comparisons. These changes concern actual reported comparison entries, not citations alone.

E3.justification: v2 adds a matched 1.4B Rodimus–Mamba2 experiment using 100B Pile tokens and the same tokenizer, plus recall evaluation with 1024-token inputs and a 512-token generation limit. It introduces batch-one efficiency measurements at 4K/24K contexts. The practical-model evaluation changes from a 2.5T-token 1.6B model to approximately 8T-token Coder models at 1.6B and 4B, including base and Chat variants.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Pile memory-budget sensitivity study (Table 7), a Rodimus/SW-SKA/FFN ordering ablation (Table 18), and training/inference FLOPs, throughput, and memory analyses (Tables 19–20). The retained head-compression ablation gains cache-memory measurements in Table 14. Existing gate, rank, expansion-factor, and residual ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The retained MQAR practice of selecting the best accuracy across learning-rate settings is unchanged.

E6.justification: Most inherited results, including Table 1 and the NeedleBench plots, are unchanged. New Table 10 reports average accuracy of 49.73 for Rodimus versus 49.24 for Mamba2 under matched 1.4B/100B-token conditions; Table 11 reports 52.30 for Rodimus+ versus 48.52 for Pythia. Efficiency results and the replacement Coder tables substantially expand the evidence, with Coder scores obtained under different training conditions from v1.

T1.justification: Table 4 corrects Rodimus's input matrix B_t by replacing the all-ones factor with beta-hat_t, bringing the summary formula into agreement with Equation 11 already present in v1. Proposition 1, its selection lemma and proof, the SKA derivation, and the chunkwise derivations otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: DDTS-based Rodimus, the SW-SKA hybrid Rodimus+, and improved accuracy–memory trade-offs. The shorter conclusion and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these core scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for Rodimus+'s data requirements when dividing global and local modeling between components (D.2), and for depth-dependent sensitivity to block ordering (D.10). Appendix E.1 distinguishes low FLOPs/cache requirements from practical throughput limitations and attributes slower inference to missing I/O optimizations. The original Future Work limitations are retained after relocation.

D1.justification: The abstract changes a promised future release into a reported code/checkpoint release with access information. v2 additionally documents WikiText model dimensions, layer/parameter accounting, memory-curve construction, Coder training-stage budgets and data proportions, and checkpoint/evaluation-script locations. These are substantial documentation and access changes; the linked resources were not independently accessed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for contemporary coding models and benchmarks, including Qwen2.5-Coder, Gemma3, Phi-4-Mini, and Ling-Coder, and adds discussion of recurrent-model adoption. The foundational positioning against gated linear attention, SSMs, sparse attention, and existing hybrid architectures remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely preserved. v2 adds explanatory summaries, revises cross-references, reorganizes the practical-model section into base/chat subsections, and moves Future Work from Appendix A to G. These are localized editorial and structural changes alongside the separately assessed scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout and extensively resizes and redistributes retained figures and tables. It adds several evaluation and efficiency tables, expands the head-compression table with a memory column, and replaces v1's compact practical-results table with separate, substantially larger base/chat tables. The original figures are retained rather than constituting new analyses.

improvement.justification: v1's larger-model comparisons were confounded by different training data and budgets, and efficiency evidence emphasized asymptotics and memory/perplexity curves. v2 materially strengthens assessment through the matched 1.4B comparison, broader recall tests, and measured throughput/FLOPs/cache results. The latter expose an important limitation: Rodimus achieves 21.4 words/s versus Mamba2's 59.3 despite using less cache. Added ablations and documented resource access further improve support and reproducibility. Coder results involve changed training and some publication-sourced baselines, and broad efficiency wording remains, but the gains in evidence and transparency are substantial.
